claims.text: Superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy alloys is governed by the degree of atomic size mismatch.
Atomic size mismatch enhances lattice disorder.
Lattice disorder alters the electron-phonon coupling involved in Cooper-pair formation.
A fixed-valence-electron-count HEA with minimal atomic size mismatch provides a low-lattice-disorder baseline.
Atomic size mismatch can be systematically increased by substituting elements having increasingly different atomic radii while holding the overall electron count constant.
Superconducting Tc can be determined at cryogenic temperatures using transport and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.
Increasing atomic size mismatch induces enhanced local lattice distortions.
Enhanced lattice disorder modifies the phonon density of states.
Enhanced lattice disorder increases electron scattering.
Changes in the phonon density of states and electron scattering alter electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling controls Cooper-pair formation in the relevant superconducting HEAs.
Greater lattice disorder is expected to suppress superconducting transition temperature.
At fixed electron count, alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have lower Tc than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
The predicted reduction in Tc results from lattice disorder interfering with electron-phonon interactions favorable to superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate only while electron count remains constant.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate if disorder causes localization or a structural or electronic phase transition.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening or electron microscopy can be used to characterize lattice disorder in the comparison series.
The hypothesis is falsified if increased-mismatch samples lack a statistically significant reduction in Tc or if measured disorder does not correlate with Tc modulation.
